text:
NORTH CAROLINA INDUSTRIAL COMMISSION

I.C. NO. 19-023663, BRIAN HALL, Employee, Plaintiff v. JONES LANG LASALLE,

INC., Employer, HARTFORD UNDERWRITERS INSURANCE COMPANY, Carrier,

Defendants.

OPINION AND AWARD for the Full Commission by KENNETH L. GOODMAN,

Commissioner.

Filed: August 8, 2024

This case was heard before the Full Commission on April 17, 2024, upon the parties’

cross appeal of the Opinion and Award filed by Deputy Commissioner Thomas H. Perlungher on

October 31, 2023. The evidentiary hearing which resulted in the Opinion & Award currently on

review before this panel was conducted on January 20, 2023. The deposition transcripts of

David Musante, M.D., and Shepherd Rosenblum, M.D., are part of the evidence of record.

A P P E A R A N C E S

Plaintiff: Bowman Law, PLLC, Winston-Salem, North Carolina;

Joseph S. Bowman, appearing.

Defendants: Hedrick Gardner Kincheloe & Garofalo, LLP, Raleigh, North Carolina;

Charles E. Vail, appearing.

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission has reviewed the prior Opinion and Award based upon the record

of the proceedings before the Deputy Commissioner, the parties’ respective Form 44s

Applications for Review

, and the briefs and arguments of the parties. The Full Commission

hereby enters the following Opinion and Award pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-85:

* * * * * * * * * * *

PRELIMINARY MATTERS

The evidentiary hearing before the former Deputy Commissioner occurred on January 20,

2023. At that time, Plaintiff had not yet been evaluated by Kevin Speer, M.D., for a second

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 2

opinion evaluation. On January 20, 2023, Deputy Commissioner Perlungher filed an Order

establishing the deadlines for the completion of post-hearing depositions, contentions, and

proposed Opinion and Awards. Pursuant to Deputy Commissioner Perlungher’s post-hearing

scheduling Order, the parties were “allowed ninety (90) days from the date of the hearing in

which to submit all evidence, including depositions” and “evidence in this matter is to be

completed by

20 April 2023

.”

On March 23, 2023, Plaintiff underwent a second opinion evaluation, pursuant to North

Carolina General Statute § 97-27(b) with Dr. Speer. Dr. Speer found that Plaintiff was at

maximum medical improvement (“MMI”) and assigned a twenty-five percent (25%) permanent

partial impairment (“PPI”) rating to Plaintiff’s left arm.

On April 20, 2023, Plaintiff filed a

Motion to Supplement the Record

requesting that the

Commission admit Dr. Speer’s dictated note from March 23, 2023. Plaintiff sought the inclusion

of this medical record “in the event Defendants contend the payment of a disability rating is

appropriate following the hearing in this matter; however, Plaintiff maintains his contention as to

the lack of suitable employment offered by Defendants . . . .” Additionally, on April 28, 2023,

Plaintiff filed

Employee-Plaintiff’s Motion for Reimbursement of a Second Opinion Examination

Pursuant to N.C.G.S. § 97-27(b)

seeking an order compelling Defendants to pay the costs of

Plaintiff’s second opinion examination with Dr. Speer.

On May 1, 2023, Defendants filed

Defendants’ Response to Motion to Supplement the

Record

objecting to Plaintiff’s motion. In their response, Defendants contended that Plaintiff’s

request to supplement the record was untimely for not seeking a second opinion evaluation

sooner, and violated Industrial Commission Rule 607. Defendants argued that they would be

prejudiced by allowing the medical record into evidence and

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 3

to cure any incurred prejudice, Defendants would need to be

permitted at Plaintiff’s cost to have the right to recall Plaintiff,

notice a second deposition of Dr. Rosenblum and notice the

deposition of Dr. Speer.

Plaintiff’s

Reply

to

Defendants’ Response to Motion to Supplement the Record

, filed on

May 3, 2023, again requested that Dr. Speer’s note be included in evidence as the record had not

yet closed. Further, Plaintiff’s

Reply

states that

Defendants’ assertions as to any “violation” of the Pre-Trial Order

or [d]iscovery rules in this case are without grounds. Plaintiff[]

sought, and ultimately obtained, a medical opinion to which he is

entitled by N.C.G.S. § 97-27(b), despite every effort by Defendants

to prevent him from doing so. He has now supplied the

corresponding medical documentation to Defendants, and has

respectfully requested that it be introduced and included within the

record of this matter.

Plaintiff’s

Reply

indicated that Plaintiff consented to “giving additional lay testimony, to the

taking of additional deposition testimony of Dr. Rosenblum . . . and Dr. Speer.” However,

Plaintiff did not agree to assuming the costs for this additional testimony.

On May 4, 2023, Deputy Commissioner Perlungher filed an Order granting Plaintiff’s

Motion to Supplement the Evidence of Record

and admitting Dr. Speer’s dictated note of March

28, 2023, as Plaintiff’s Exhibit #1. Deputy Commissioner Perlungher’s Order additionally

permitted Defendants “to recall [P]laintiff for deposition, notice a second deposition of Dr.

Rosenblum, and notice the deposition of Dr. Speer.”

On May 8, 2023, Defendants responded to Plaintiff’s

Motion for Reimbursement of a

Second Opinion Examination pursuant to N.C.G.S. § 97-27(b)

. Defendants argued that they

should not be required to reimburse Plaintiff for the second opinion appointment because he had

not previously provided sufficient proof of dissatisfaction with the prior rating assigned by Dr.

Rosenblum.

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 4

On May 12, 2023, Deputy Commissioner Perlungher filed an Order granting Plaintiff’s

request for reimbursement for the cost of the second opinion examination. On June 29, 2023,

Deputy Commissioner Perlungher filed an Order closing the record.

In their brief to the Full Commission, Defendants argue that Deputy Commissioner

Perlungher erred by admitting Dr. Speer’s dictated note of March 28, 2023, and ordering

Defendants to reimburse Plaintiff for the second opinion evaluation performed by Dr. Speer.

Defendants request that the Full Commission vacate Deputy Commissioner Perlungher’s Orders

of May 4, 2023, and May 12, 2023.

A.

Motion to Supplement Record

Pursuant to 11 NCAC 23A. 0701(i) “[a]fter a request for review has been submitted to

the Full Commission, any motions related to the issues for review shall be filed with the Full

Commission . . . .” Generally, such motions are considered by the Full Commission at the time

of review of the appeal.

Id.

On review of a workers’ compensation award, the North Carolina

Industrial Commission has plenary power to receive additional evidence and may do so at its

sound discretion. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-85 (2023);

Lynch v. M.B. Kahn Constr. Co.

, 41 N.C. App.

127, 130-31, 254 S.E.2d 236, 238 (1979).

Here, the medical record from Dr. Speer did not exist at the time of the hearing before the

Deputy Commissioner. Plaintiff timely filed a motion seeking its inclusion prior to the close of

the evidentiary record. Thereafter, Defendants were afforded an opportunity to take additional

testimony and depose Drs. Rosenblum and Speer. For these reasons, and in the discretion of the

Full Commission, Deputy Commissioner Perlungher’s Order admitting Dr. Speer’s dictated note

of March 28, 2023, into evidence as Plaintiff’s Exhibit #1 is AFFIRMED.

B.

Motion for Reimbursement of a Second Opinion Examination pursuant to

N.C.G.S. § 97-27(b)

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 5

North Carolina General Statute § 97-27(b) allows an employee, when dissatisfied with an

assigned disability rating, to seek “another examination solely on the percentage of permanent

disability provided by a duly qualified physician of the employee’s choosing . . . .” N.C. Gen.

Stat. § 97-27(b) (2023). The employer is statutorily required to cover the cost of this

examination “in the same manner as health care providers designated by the employer or the

Industrial Commission are paid.” Id.

Defendants contend that Plaintiff failed to appropriately or timely express dissatisfaction

with the rating assigned by Dr. Rosenblum. In particular, Defendants’ brief states that

“Plaintiff’s proclamation of dissatisfaction is insufficient proof of dissatisfaction and

incongruous with his actions.”

However, in this case, Plaintiff’s counsel stated in his

Reply

that any delay was a “direct

result of Defendants’ denial of Plaintiff’s [s]econd [o]pinion [r]equests throughout the pendency

of this case . . . .” Further, Plaintiff has asserted his right to a second opinion examination with

the timeframe permitted under North Carolina General Statute § 97-25.1. Finally, the statutory

requirements contained within North Carolina General Statute § 97-27(b) do not contain a

specified manner of expressing dissatisfaction with an assigned impairment rating, and it is not

the Commission’s role to expand or create the statutory language requiring an employee to assert

dissatisfaction with a rating in any other manner except as specifically delineated in North

Carolina General Statute § 97-27(b).

Based on the foregoing, the Commission hereby AFFIRMS Deputy Commissioner

Perlungher’s Order of May 12, 2023, granting Plaintiff’s request for reimbursement for the cost

of the second opinion examination.

The Full Commission addresses the following:

ISSUES

1.

Did Plaintiff sustain a compensable injury to his cervical spine at work on May

30, 2019?

2.

Is the operating engineer job suitable employment?

3.

Are Defendants entitled to a credit pursuant to North Carolina General Statute §

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 8

97-42?

4.

Whether Defendants must provide vocational rehabilitation services?

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based upon the preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record, and

reasonable inferences flowing therefrom, the Full Commission makes the following:

FINDINGS OF FACT

1.

As of the date of the hearing before the Deputy Commissioner, Plaintiff was 57

years old, and a resident of Louisburg, North Carolina. Plaintiff was hired by Defendant-

Employer, an international facilities management company, on January 15, 2018, as an operating

engineer. Defendant-Employer’s employees are assigned various work locations. Plaintiff’s

assigned workplace was the ABB transformer plant (“ABB”) in Pinetops, North Carolina.

2.

Plaintiff’s job as an operating engineer required him to operate, maintain,

troubleshoot, and repair facility equipment. Operating engineers employed by Defendant-

Employer were “expected to demonstrate technical expertise in one craft area (Electrical, HVAC,

Piping/Plumbing, Central Utility Plant Operations) and be multi-skilled in others in order to

successfully complete daily/weekly work assignments.” The job description, produced by

Defendants, for the operating engineer states that the position requires the capacity to lift up to

35 pounds, an “[a]bility to bend, sit, squat, stand, reach, and lay as required to access equipment

components for extended periods of time,” and an “[a]bility to work exposed to heat, sunlight,

rain, cold, daylight, and nighttime hours as required.”

3.

According to Plaintiff, the operating engineer position requires him to “take care

of any facility maintenance[,]” including HVAC, plumbing, electrical, masonry, carpentry, and

I.C. NO. 19-023663

Page 9

roof maintenance or repairs. Plaintiff testified that the job required him to lift over 100 pounds,

and involved significant ladder work, climbing, and overhead work. On occasion, Plaintiff

hauled equipment to the roof. Plaintiff characterized the job as a “heavy duty job.”

4.

On May 30, 2019, Plaintiff sustained an injury to his left shoulder at work while

preventing an air circulator fan from falling. At the time of the injury, Plaintiff was standing in

an industrial lift, raised to the ceiling. Plaintiff was tethered to the lift for fall protection.

Plaintiff was placing a fan motor on a pedestal over an oven, when the fan, weighing

approximately 50 to 60 pounds, fell. Plaintiff testified that when he caught the fan, he felt a pull

from his neck through his shoulder. Plaintiff immediately reported the injury to Defendant-

Employer’s maintenance manager, Sherwood McKeel, and his supervisor, Dave Nassert.

5.

Likewise, Defendant-Employer’s Form 19

Employer’s Report of Employee’s

Injury or Occupational Disease to the Industrial Commission

states that Plaintiff “was replacing

an air circulator, [and] during the installation of the fan, the fan fell, and [Plaintiff] caught it with

his left arm, causing pain to the left shoulder.”

6.

On June 5, 2019, Plaintiff presented to Jessica Jones, PA, at FastMed Urgent Care

and reported left shoulder pain resulting from an incident at work on May 30, 2019, when “[h]e

was installing a 125 lb fan with a coworker when they lost control of the fan and it fell . . . [and

he] caught it with his left hand.” X-ray imaging of Plaintiff’s left shoulder revealed “no factures

or avulsions.” PA Jones provided Plaintiff with a sling for his left arm and work restrictions of

“[r]ight-handed duty only.” Plaintiff returned to FastMed Urgent Care on June 7, 2019,

reporting severe, aching left shoulder pain. The provider indicated that Plaintiff may need an

MRI to “[r]ule out left rotator cuff pathology.”

7.

While the most significant pain was in his left shoulder, Plaintiff testified that he

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 10

felt a shocking sensation in his neck and had numbness in his right hand following the incident

on May 30, 2019. However, the medical records from FastMed Urgent Care indicate that

Plaintiff’s neck had “good range of motion,” and “no pain on cervical compression.”

8.

On June 13, 2019, Plaintiff presented to Shepherd Rosenblum, MD, at Triangle

Orthopedics in Durham, North Carolina. The dictated note for this encounter states that Plaintiff

“was operating a man-lift while putting in an air rotator fan . . . when the fan slipped[,] and he

jerked his left shoulder when trying to catch it. He heard and felt a snap in his left shoulder,

followed by immediate pain.” Plaintiff reported pain with his usual activities of daily living,

sharp pain in his left shoulder through his elbow, and difficulty sleeping due to pain. On

examination, Dr. Rosenblum noted that Plaintiff had “positive drop-arm on the left” and

“[m]arkedly positive and secondary impingement signs.” Dr. Rosenblum ordered an MRI of

Plaintiff’s left shoulder and assigned work restrictions of “no active use of the left upper

extremity.” The note for this visit does not mention neck pain.

9.

On June 14, 2019, Defendants filed a Form 63

Notice to Employee of Payment of

Compensation Without Prejudice (G.S. § 97-18(d)) or Payment of Medical Benefits Only Without

Prejudice (G.S. § 97-2(19) & § 97-25)

and selected “Section 1: Indemnity Benefits[,]” indicating

that Defendants were initiating indemnity and medical compensation for Plaintiff’s left shoulder

injury and reserving the right to subsequently deny the claim, within 90 days, pending

Defendants’ investigation of the claim. As stipulated in the Pre-Trial Agreement, Defendants

accept the compensability of Plaintiff’s left shoulder injury sustained on May 30, 2019.

10.

The MRI of Plaintiff’s left shoulder, taken on June 20, 2019, revealed a “high-

grade tear involving mid to anterior supraspinatus tendinous insertion with . . . full thickness

component at anterior margin . . . .” On June 25, 2019, after reviewing the MRI, Dr. Rosenblum

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 11

noted Plaintiff sustained a “20-mm high-grade tear with predominantly 70-80% thickness . . .

[and] significant impingement of the AC joint.” Dr. Rosenblum recommended that Plaintiff

undergo a left shoulder arthroscopy.

11.

On July 24, 2019, Plaintiff underwent a left shoulder arthroscopy with rotator cuff

repair, biceps tenodesis, subacromial decompression, resection of distal clavicle, and extensive

debridement performed by Dr. Rosenblum. Thereafter, Plaintiff completed a course of physical

therapy but noticed that his “arm was locking and popping.” On February 12, 2020, Plaintiff

underwent a revision surgery to his left shoulder repair performed by Dr. Rosenblum. When the

left shoulder symptoms persisted after the second surgery, Dr. Rosenblum performed a third

surgery on January 20, 2021.

12.

On August 20, 2020, Plaintiff filed a Form 18

Notice of Accident to Employer and

Claim of Employee, Representative, or Dependent (G.S. §§ 97-22 through 24)

indicating that he

sustained a left shoulder and arm injury on May 30, 2019, while installing an air circulation fan

and motor. The Form 18 does not list a cervical or neck injury.

13.

On July 27, 2021, Plaintiff presented to CORA Physical Therapy where he

underwent a functional capacity evaluation (

“

FCE

”

). The physical therapist noted that Plaintiff

demonstrated consistent and maximal effort, with a correlation between the test

results and

diagnosis, and as a result the “FCE is a reliable indication of his true functional

abilities . . .

.”

The results of the FCE reflected that P

laintiff is able to: lift floor to waist up to 30

pounds

occasionally; lift 12” to knuckle up to

40 pounds occasionally; lift waist to chest up to 35 pounds

occasionally; lift waist to shoulder up to 15 pounds occasionally; carry up to 35 pounds

occasionally; and can only minimally crawl due to increased pain with weight bearing.

14.

On August 24, 2021, Plaintiff filed a Form 33

Request that Claim be Assigned for

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 12

Hearing

stating that “Plaintiff is not receiving workers’ compensation benefits to which he is

entitled.”

15.

On August 26, 2021, Dr. Rosenblum reviewed the results of the FCE and

endorsed the permanent restrictions as recommended by the FCE provider. On September 16,

2021, Dr. Rosenblum completed a Form 25R

Evaluation for Permanent Impairment

, placed

Plaintiff at MMI, and

assigned a PPI rating to P

laintiff’s left arm of

fifteen percent (15%).

16.

Following his May 30, 2019, left shoulder injury, Plaintiff returned to work on

June 11, 2019. Thereafter, Plaintiff returned to work for Defendant-Employer after each

shoulder surgery. Following his July 24, 2019, shoulder surgery, Plaintiff returned to work on

July 1, 2019; following his February 12, 2020, surgery, Plaintiff returned to work on April 21,

2020, and following his January 20, 2021, surgery, Plaintiff returned to work on March 9, 2021.

Each time, Plaintiff returned to work in his former job as an operating engineer, with

modifications, earning the same or greater wages.

17.

Plaintiff’s modified position includes the use of a helper, who Plaintiff manages,

and who completes tasks Plaintiff is physically unable to perform. Prior to his May 30, 2019

injury, Plaintiff was not provided a helper to complete the physical duties of his job as an

operating engineer. Plaintiff testified that he is not aware of any other operating engineer who is

allowed to have a helper and he believes he is the only one with such an accommodation. In the

event the helper is not available, Plaintiff attempts to delay the work until the helper is available,

or attempts to use a third-party contractor, Mobile Engineering Services (“MES”).

18.

However, there are times when ABB requires immediate assistance, and Plaintiff

is required to accommodate these requests even if the helper or MES are unavailable and the

tasks are outside of his permanent work restrictions. Even with the modifications, there are

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 13

certain aspects of the operating engineer position that Plaintiff remains physically unable to

complete (i.e. lifting, overhead work, and use of a fall protection harness which is painful for

Plaintiff’s left shoulder). In particular, Plaintiff testified that his job requires him, at times, to

change overhead air filters, install large televisions over his head, and drive large signposts into

the ground. Plaintiff testified that each of these tasks are “very, very difficult” for him to

perform.

19.

Plaintiff further testified that he very much liked working for Defendant-

Employer and returned to work in hopes of finding a position with Defendant-Employer within

his permanent restrictions. Additionally, Plaintiff testified that, in his absence, Defendant-

Employer would hire MES to perform the operating engineer job duties, and this decreases the

location’s profitability.

20.

On September 29, 2021, Defendants filed a Form 61

Denial of Workers’

Compensation Claim (G.S. § 97-18(c) and G.S. § 97-18(d))

denying that Plaintiff “sustained any

compensable injury on May 30, 2019 beyond that very injury involving the left shoulder

admitted by way of the June 14, 2019 Form 63 – Section 1” and specifically denying “any

cervical condition should Employee-Plaintiff claim the same.” Despite the foregoing,

Defendants “agreed to provide [a] cervical evaluation voluntarily and without prejudice under

the Form 63 Section 2 filed contemporaneously.”

21.

On October 11, 2021, Plaintiff presented to David Musante, M.D., of Triangle

Orthopedics, at D

efendants’ direction, for an examination related to Plaintiff’s neck complaints

.

Dr. Musante noted that Plaintiff “had long-term treatment on his left shoulder but had persistent

symptoms that [Dr.] Rosenblum thought could be related to his neck.” Plaintiff reported to Dr.

Musante that “except for his pain in his shoulder, he is fine.” Plaintiff further reported that “he is

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 14

not suffering enough that he would want to have any surgery on his neck . . . .” On examination,

Dr. Musante noted that Plaintiff had full range of motion of the neck without pain. Dr. Musante

reviewed an MRI of Plaintiff’s cervical spine, taken on September 9, 2021, and noted an

abnormality at C5-C6 but noted that “I do not think this is causing him any symptoms.”

22.

On January 19, 2023, Plaintiff filed an Amended Form 18 to include Plaintiff’s

cervical spine as a listed injury resulting from the May 30, 2019, incident at work.

23.

On January 20, 2023, Plaintiff and Robert Vaughn testified at the hearing before

Deputy Commissioner Perlungher.

Plaintiff testified that the operating engineer job description

produced by Defendants detailing the job duties and physical requirements of the position was

inaccurate and incomplete. In particular, Plaintiff testified that the position requires him to lift

more than 35 pounds. Plaintiff further testified that the job description omits the climbing,

overhead work, and crawling duties, all of which were necessary to complete the operating

engineer job. The job description produced by Defendants does not specify that it is specific to

the Pinetops, North Carolina ABB location.

24.

Plaintiff testified that his neck pain has been constant since the May 30, 2019,

incident at work. According to Plaintiff, his neck pain is worse when he turns his neck or if he

looks down for a long time. At the hearing, Plaintiff was not experiencing any neck pain.

25.

Plaintiff testified that he would prefer to remain employed by Defendants.

Plaintiff further testified that he would need retraining, and vocational assistance, to find a job

within his permanent restrictions.

26.

Mr. Vaughn is a Senior Facilities Manager employed by Defendant-Employer and

is Plaintiff’s supervisor. Mr. Vaughn confirmed that Defendant-Employer is financially

incentivized to bring Plaintiff back to work as quickly as possible to offset the costs of using

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 15

outside MES services.

27.

Mr. Vaughn testified that Plaintiff’s job as operating engineer was modified to

accommodate P

laintiff’s

permanent restrictions. In particular, Mr. Vaughn explained that a

second operating engineer was hired to assist Plaintiff with his job beginning in January of 2022.

Mr. Vaughn testified that Defendant-Employer

“justified” modifying the job by

hiring an

assistant for Plaintiff and by requiring the assistant to have HVAC expertise. This justification

was necessary as typically Defendant-Employer would not be able to hire an additional person

without reducing expenses. Mr. Vaughn testified that he is aware that Plaintiff requires

assistance from a

helper to perform physical tasks

.

Mr. Vaughn explained that the helper was

hired to specifically work with Plaintiff and for his technical expertise.

Mr. Vaughn was not able

to testify to the existence of any lighter duty roles

available to Plaintiff with Defendant-

Employer.

28.

On March 28, 2023, Plaintiff presented to Kevin Speer, M.D., of Southeastern

Orthopedics Shoulder Center for a second opinion rating evaluation. Dr. Speer agreed with Dr.

Rosenblum that Plaintiff is at MMI and agreed with the restrictions assigned. Dr. Speer

indicated that based on P

laintiff’s

three surgical procedures, and

Plaintiff’s ongoing pain and

weakness, a PPI rating of twenty-five percent

(25%) for Plaintiff’s left shoulder was appropriate.

29.

Dr. Rosenblum is a board-certified

orthopedic surgeon and was tendered at his

deposition as an expert in orthopedic medicine and

orthopedic surgery and is accepted as such.

According to Dr. Rosenblum, Plaintiff’s permanent work restrictions, related to his left shoulder

injury, include a limitation on lifting floor to waist up to 30

pounds, lifting waist to chest up to

35 pounds, lifting waist to shoulder up to 15 pounds, and

carrying up to 35 pounds occasionally.

Dr. Rosenblum confirmed that Plaintiff's restrictions prevent him

from lifting anything from the

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 16

ground that weighs over 30 pounds, and that Plaintiff cannot lift

anything over his waist

weighing 15 pounds more than occasionally.

30.

Dr. Rosenblum

clarified that the permanent restrictions enumerated within his

August 26, 2021, medical record were not exhaustive, and that P

laintiff’s physical restrictions

include additional limitations,

including a preclusion of overheard work and lifting, as well as

crawling. Dr. Rosenblum also restricted Plaintiff from using a harness, or any fall protection

device that put direct pressure on Plaintiff’s left shoulder or caused shoulder pain. Dr.

Rosenblum indicated that Plaintiff should be

further prohibited from any sustained use of the arm

above 90 degrees, and should use his left arm only

occasionally, even up to 120 degrees.

31.

Dr. Rosenblum opined that Plaintiff attained MMI and he did not anticipate any

meaningful improvement in P

laintiff’s permanent,

functional limitations and work restrictions.

Dr. Rosenblum opined that Plaintiff was unable to satisfy the physical

requirements of the

operating engineer position.

32.

Dr. Rosenblum testified that he documents his patients’ pertinent complaints, and

based on his medical records, March 19, 2020, was the first time Plaintiff presented with

complaints of tingling in his right hand, and August 26, 2021, was the first examination date that

Plaintiff presented with any neck complaints. When asked by Plaintiff’s counsel whether

Plaintiff’s neck pain was related to the May 30, 2019, incident at work, Dr. Rosenblum replied

that he could not answer that question. Dr. Rosenblum explained that Plaintiff did not have neck

complaints following the initial injury, and while “[i]t’s certainly possible that this is a separate

arising incident[,]” he could not comment on the neck injury. Dr. Rosenblum explained that if

the neck pain was related to the use of the left arm sling, the pain should have resolved by now.

However, he further explained that “the sling itself would not have caused the disc issue” as seen

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 17

on the cervical MRI.

33.

Dr. Musante is a board-certified

orthopedic surgeon and was tendered as an expert

in orthopedic medicine and is accepted as such.

Dr. Musante acknowledged that the mechanism

of catching an item weighing 50

to 60 pounds is enough to cause sprains and strains of

musculoskeletal structures and “could have been something that was sufficient to activate

previously asymptomatic pathology.” He

also testified P

laintiff more likely than not had

preexisting degeneration in his neck because, “the

pathology was --

had a chronic appearance to

it[,]” and “someone in their early 50s is expected to have pathology such as this in their neck.”

34.

Dr. Musante evaluated Plaintiff on October 11, 2021, over two years after the

shoulder injury sustained on May 30, 2019. Dr. Musante recalled that Plaintiff’s neck injury was

“pretty minor” and that Plaintiff did not report any radicular symptoms or much pain. When

Plaintiff’s counsel asked Dr. Musante whether it was more likely than not that the May 30, 2019,

accident at work caused Plaintiff’s neck pain, Dr. Musante responded

[y]es . . . [so] long as he didn’t have neck pain before the injury

and he began to have neck pain after the injury . . . within a short

time frame. Not like two years later or a year and a half later, but

within a - - you know, within 24 to 48 hours would be a reasonable

amount of time.

35.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1.

On May 30, 2019, Plaintiff sustained an admittedly compensable injury by

accident resulting in injury to his left shoulder arising out of and in the course of his employment

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 21

with Defendant-Employer. N.C. Gen. Stat.§ 97-2(6) (2023).

2.

In workers’ compensation cases, the plaintiff has the burden of proving every

element of compensability. As part of this burden, the plaintiff must present a preponderance of

evidence in view of the entire record establishing these elements.

Whitfield v. Lab. Corp. of Am.

,

158 N.C. App. 341, 350, 581 S.E.2d 778, 784 (2003);

Harvey v. Raleigh Police Dep’t

, 96 N.C.

App. 28, 35, 384. S.E.2d 549, 553, disc. rev. denied, 325 N.C. 706, 388 S.E.2d 454 (1989). The

Industrial Commission is the sole judge of the credibility of witnesses.

Adams v. AVX Corp.

, 349

N.C. 676, 680, 509 S.E.2d 411, 413 (1998).

3.

A compensable injury to the spine can be proven by establishing that it occurred

as the result of an “injury by accident” or as the result of a “specific traumatic incident.”

See

Caskie v. R.M. Butler & Co.

, 85 N.C. App. 266, 268, 354 S.E.2d 242, 244 (1987). The Workers’

Compensation Act provides that:

[w]ith respect to back injuries . . . where injury to the back arises

out of and in the course of the employment and is the direct result

of a specific traumatic incident of the work assigned, ‘injury by

accident’ shall be construed to include any disabling physical

injury to the back arising out of and causally related to such

incident.

N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-2(6) (2023). To prove a specific traumatic incident, a plaintiff must show

the injury occurred at a judicially cognizable point in time and it did not develop gradually.

Chambers v. Transit Mgmt

., 360 N.C. 609, 618–19, 636 S.E.2d 553, 558–59 (2006). The onset

of pain, without more, does not establish evidence of a specific traumatic incident.

Id.

4.

Furthermore, in addition to establishing the existence of a compensable event, an

employee must also prove a causal relationship between that event and the condition for which

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 22

he seeks compensation.

Holley v. ACTS, Inc

., 357 N.C. 228, 231–32, 581 S.E.2d 750, 752

(2003). Plaintiff must provide evidence of causation and the evidence “must be such as to take

the case out of the realm of conjecture and remote possibility.”

Gilmore v. Hoke Cty. Bd. of

Educ.

, 222 N.C. 358, 365, 23 S.E.2d 292, 296 (1942). “[W]here the exact nature and probable

genesis of a particular type of injury involves complicated medical questions far removed from

the ordinary experience and knowledge of laymen, only an expert can give competent opinion

evidence as to the cause of the injury.

Click v. Pilot Freight Carriers, Inc.

, 300 N.C. 164, 167,

265 S.E.2d 389, 391 (1980). Expert testimony is required, and it cannot be based on speculation,

mere possibility or purely a temporal relationship between the accident and the condition.

Young

v. Hickory Bus. Furniture

, 353 N.C. 227, 230-33, 538 S.E.2d 912, 915-16 (2000). “Could” or

“might” expert testimony is insufficient to support a causal connection when there is additional

evidence or testimony showing the expert’s opinion to be a guess or mere speculation.

5.

In the present matter, Plaintiff has failed to establish that he suffered a

compensable injury by accident and/or specific traumatic incident on May 30, 2019, resulting in

injury to his cervical spine. Given the complicated medical issues present, only an expert can

provide competent evidence as to the causal relationship between Plaintiff’s cervical spine

condition and his work-related incident on May 30, 2019.

Click

, 300 N.C. at 167, 265 S.E.2d at

391;

Young

, 353 N.C. at 230-33, 538 S.E.2d at 915-16. Plaintiff’s expert witness, Dr.

Rosenblum, declined to provide an expert opinion on causation, and Dr. Musante’s testimony

was equivocal and based on a temporal relation reported by Plaintiff. Plaintiff called no

additional experts to opine on the issue of causation prior to the close of the record.

Accordingly, the Commission concludes that Plaintiff has failed to establish that he suffered a

compensable cervical spine injury as a result of the incident at work on May 30, 2019, and

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 23

therefore his cervical spine injury claim must be denied.

Id.

6.

Disability is defined as “incapacity because of injury to earn the wages which the

employee was receiving at the time of injury in the same or any other employment.” N.C. Gen.

Stat. 97-2(9) (2023). An injured employee is not entitled to disability compensation if he

unjustifiably refuses suitable employment. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-32 (2023). To demonstrate that

an injured employee has the ability to earn pre-injury wages in the same employment after

reaching MMI, and therefore is not entitled to disability compensation, Defendants must offer

the injured employee “suitable employment” that accurately demonstrates the employee’s ability

to earn wages in the competitive job market. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-2(22) (2023);

Peoples v. Cone

Mills Corp.

, 316 N.C. 426, 437, 342 S.E.2d 798, 806 (1986);

Saums v. Raleigh Cmty. Hosp.

, 346

N.C. 760, 763-65, 487 S.E.2d 746, 749-50 (1997). The fact that an employee is capable of

performing (or attempts to perform) employment tendered by the employer is not, as a matter of

law, an indication of the employee’s ability to earn wages.

Saums

, 346 N.C. at 764, 487 S.E.2d

at 750 (citing

Peoples

, 316 N.C. at 434, 342 S.E.2d at 804). An employer may not establish an

employee’s capacity to earn his pre-injury wages in the same employment “by showing that the

employee is capable of earning pre-injury wages in a temporary position, or by creating a

position within the employer’s own company which is not ordinarily available in the competitive

job market, because such positions do not accurately reflect the employee’s capacity to earn

wages.”

Stamey v. North Carolina Self-Ins. Guar. Ass'n

, 131 N.C. App. 662, 666, 507 S.E.2d

596, 599 (1998) (internal citations and quotation marks omitted);

see also Saums

, 346 N.C. at

765, 487 S.E.2d at 750;

Smith v. Sealed Air Corp.

, 127 N.C. App. 359, 362, 489 S.E.2d 445, 447

(1997). “The Workers’ Compensation Act does not permit [defendants] to avoid [their] duty to

pay compensation by offering an injured employee employment which the employee under

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 24

normally prevailing market conditions could find nowhere else and which [defendants] could

terminate at will or . . . for reasons beyond [their] control.”

Peoples

, 316 N.C. at 439, 342 S.E.2d

at 806;

Saums,

346 N.C. at 765, 487 S.E.2d at 750;

Smith,

127 N.C. App. at 362, 489 S.E.2d at

447 (noting that “the employer must come forward with evidence that others would hire the

employee ‘to do a similar job at a comparable wage’”). Defendants have the burden to show that

a proffered job is suitable employment.

Munns v. Precision Franchising, Inc.

, 196 N.C. App.

315, 317-18, 674 S.E.2d 430, 433 (2009).

7.

Plaintiff contends the operating engineer position is not suitable post-MMI

employment because it is not within his permanent work restrictions. Plaintiff further contends

the evidence of record fails to establish that the modified position of the operating engineer with

an assistant is available in the competitive marketplace and thus representative of Plaintiff’s

earning capacity. Defendants contend that the operating engineer position is suitable

employment such that Plaintiff is not entitled to disability compensation. “Suitable

employment,” after reaching MMI, “is employment that the employee is capable of performing

considering the employee’s preexisting and injury-related physical and mental limitations,

vocational skills, education, and experience and is located within a 50-mile radius of the

employee’s residence at the time of the injury . . . .” N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-2(22) (2023). “No one

factor shall be considered exclusively in determining suitable employment.”

Id.

Here,

Defendants have failed to establish that the operating engineer position is suitable employment,

because they failed to show that the job is within Plaintiff’s injury-related physical restrictions

(i.e. lifting floor to waist 30 pounds occasionally, lifting waist to chest up to 35 pounds

occasionally, lifting waist to shoulder up to 15 pounds occasionally, and carrying up to 35

pounds occasionally). The operating engineer job description requires the ability to lift 35

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 25

pounds and the ability to “reach and lay as required to access equipment components for

extended periods of time.” Here, pursuant to the restrictions assigned by Dr. Rosenblum, and as

a result of the May 30, 2019, accident, Plaintiff cannot lift anything over his waist weighing 15

pounds more than occasionally and cannot wear a safety harness due to left shoulder pain.

Accordingly, the Commission concludes that the operating engineer position is not suitable

employment.

Id.

8.

Further, Defendants have failed to show that the operating engineer job, as

modified to accommodate Plaintiff’s restrictions by providing the use of a helper, is available in

the competitive job market. There is no vocational evidence establishing that someone with

Plaintiff’s restrictions would be hired as an operating engineer in the competitive marketplace.

Accordingly, Plaintiff is entitled to stop working the unsuitable job and begin receiving

temporary total disability compensation while he conducts a reasonable job search for suitable

employment within his restrictions. Plaintiff’s ongoing disability may be terminated by approval

of the Commission if he fails to conduct a reasonable job search or otherwise establish his

ongoing entitlement to disability compensation.

Russell v. Lowes Prod. Distrib.

, 108 N.C. App.

762, 765, 425 S.E.2d 454, 457 (1993);

Medlin v. Weaver Cooke Constr., LLC

, 367 N.C. 414,

422, 760 S.E.2d 732, 737 (2014);

Wilkes

v. City of Greenville

, 369 N.C. 730, 745, 799 S.E.2d

838, 849 (2017).

9.

Subject to the provisions of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-25.1, Plaintiff is entitled to have

Defendants provide all medical treatment, including vocational rehabilitation services, incurred

or to be incurred, necessitated by the May 30, 2019, compensable left shoulder injury when bills

for the same have been approved pursuant to Industrial Commission procedures. N.C. Gen. Stat.

§§ 97-2(19); 97- 25; 97-25.1; 97-32.2 (2023). This medical treatment shall include additional

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 26

vocational rehabilitation services. An employee may request vocational rehabilitation services,

including education and retraining, if he has not yet returned to work or is earning less than

seventy-five percent (75%) of his pre-injury average weekly wage. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-32.2

(2023). The expense of vocational rehabilitation services provided under North Carolina

General Statute Section 97-32.2 “shall be borne by the employer in the same manner as medical

compensation.”

Id.

The retraining or education must be “reasonably likely to substantially

increase the employee’s wage-earning capacity following completion of the education or

retraining program.”

Id.

At the time of the hearing, Plaintiff was employed and earning his pre-

injury wages. Accordingly, the evidence does not support Plaintiff’s request for vocational

rehabilitation services at this time.

10.

“Payments made by the employer to the injured employee during the period of his

disability . . . which by the terms of [the Workers’ Compensation Act] were not due and payable

when made, may, subject to the approval of the Commission be deducted from the amount to be

paid as compensation.” N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-42 (2023). The language of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-

42 indicates that a credit is not required to be granted. Rather, the language places the decision

of whether to grant a credit within the sound discretion of the Commission.

Moretz v. Richards

& Assocs, Inc.

, 74 N.C. App. 72, 75, 327 S.E.2d 290, 293 (1985),

aff’d as modified,

316 N.C.

539, 342 S.E.2d 844 (1986). Pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-42, and in the discretion of the

Commission, Defendants are entitled to a credit against future indemnity compensation due to

Plaintiff for indemnity payments issued to Plaintiff when otherwise not due and payable. N.C.

Gen. Stat. § 97-42 (2023). In this case, Defendants paid Plaintiff temporary total compensation

at a rate based upon an incorrect calculation of Plaintiff’s average weekly wage, to wit,

Defendants initiated disability compensation at an initial rate of $632.35. Defendants later

I.C. NO. 19-023663 Page 27

issued disability compensation at a rate of $1,028.00. Defendants contend that at Plaintiff’s

stipulated compensation rate of $773.42. Therefore, Plaintiff was overpaid indemnity

compensation in the amount of $11,395.59. Pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-42, in the case of

disability such deductions shall be made by shortening the period during which the compensation

must be paid, and not by reducing the amount of the weekly payment.
